body: It’s an attitude that’s useful whether you rent or own.Though renters may not be responsible for fixing a leaking pipe, they still have plenty to lose if something goes wrong. And while most of us know to cover the basics with smoke alarms, fire extinguishers and good locks, there are plenty of often-overlooked products that can leave you better prepared — from a fire blanket for quickly smothering a small fire to a leak sensor that alerts you when it detects water.
Below are 14 home safety and security upgrades worth considering once you’ve checked the basic boxes.

I’ve had a longtime fixation on fire safety dating back to childhood, thanks to a walkthrough house my hometown’s fire department set up to demonstrate common household fire hazards. Decades later, I still remember the lessons we were taught that day, and I’ve made a point of staying on top of new tools and products that have emerged since.

articles.title: Go with the flow: do you need to filter US tap water?
articles.summary: Experts share best practices for considering water filters – whether you’re drinking municipally treated water or relying on a well. Americans have a lot of questions about their drinking water. How is it treated? What’s in it? Most importantly, is it safe?
body: “I’ve even been out to eat where people overhear me talking about my work and come over to ask me a question about their tap water,” said Kimberly Parker, an environmental engineer who studies chemical contaminants in drinking water at Washington University in St Louis.

Most Americans have access to municipal water, which “tends to be really well treated” and largely safe to drink, said Parker. Across the US, water is monitored for contamination via centralized infrastructure at federal and state levels.
In Parker’s experience, “many environmental engineers choose not to use filtered water” because of their informed confidence in the safety of tap water, she said.
Nevertheless, whether you’re drinking municipally treated water or relying on a well, there are water-safety challenges.

articles.title: ‘In this new car, I feel patronised’: which driver assistance systems actually improve safety?
articles.summary: Modern cars are fitted with features like autonomous emergency braking and fatigue monitoring. But do they support motorists or drive them to distraction? This new car I’m test-driving boasts all the latest bells and whistles – or, rather, beeps and bings.
body: When the car determines it’s too near a white line, it tugs the wheel against my hands and brakes as a car slows ahead. Its haptic “buttons” feel like fingers pressing back – as if an invisible presence has its hands and feet on the controls: a ghost in the machine I’m inside.

Heading back to the caryard, a cryptic tone sounds. From the back seat, salesman Anthony says it’s the over-speed warning. We’re still on the 40km/h service road but the car “saw” the yard’s 5km/h speed-limit sign. Anthony advises disabling it on startup. “Most people leave it on, though,” he says. “Saves you getting done for speeding.”
But Anthony has turned off the car’s fatigue-warning feature. The car doesn’t “know” me yet, so won’t detect if I’m tired anyway. “It doesn’t like sunglasses, either,” he says.

I’ve read about some systems that are so crudely calibrated they’ll insistently demand you take a break by confusing energetic driving on a twisting mountain road with drunkenness or debility. Others declare you unfit to drive if you’ve had a cold or a rough night. You’ve already seen yourself in the bathroom mirror. Who needs a robot to rub it in?
points: Modern cars are fitted with features like autonomous emergency braking and fatigue monitoring.
But do they support motorists or drive them to distraction?

articles.title: ‘I created my mom and talk to her’: AI ghosts and deathslop are changing the way we mourn
articles.summary: The rise of AI-generated tributes and bots for ‘talking’ to the dead has experts concerned more people will grieve in isolation. Tributes rolled in after the death of Dolly Parton last month. Jack White performed Jolene at a London gig.
body: Run Jolene, at just under five minutes, is an earworm of a country song, containing all the cliches of the genre: twangy singer, banjo licks, corny lyrics. Those lyrics concern Jolene, the fictional romantic rival made infamous by Parton. “Somebody better warn Jolene / Dolly’s coming through those gates,” the voice croons. “Run Jolene / Girl you better move your feet.”

The accompanying video depicts Parton, clad in a bedazzled white jumpsuit, hunting down Jolene, a busty redhead with prom curls. Heaven is filled with deceased celebrities who watch on in horror – or amusement – as Jolene bounces from cloud to cloud, or books it up marble staircases, trying to hide from Dolly. Onlookers include the late Michael Jackson, Whitney Houston and Kenny Rogers, as well as Cher, who is still very much alive.

articles.title: This Restaurant Rocks (No, Literally)
articles.summary: A version of this post originally appeared in Eater Today, which spotlights the freshest news and stories from across the food world every day. Subscribe now. “There’s a rock in the sink!” That was the takeaway last winter after the East Coast contingent of the team that writes this newsletter met…
body: How did boulders become the hot new decor trend at New York City restaurants and cafes?

That was until I met a friend for coffee at the location of Rhythm Zero in Greenpoint, Brooklyn, which looks more like a room in an art museum than a coffee shop. There, a large hunk of stone sat in front of a large mirror next to the counter. Yet another imposed itself in the bathroom, positioned between the sink and the toilet, as though natural absorption for dripping hands making the trip to the hand dryer. Two establishments with big decorative rocks: a coincidence, or an affectation?

But then, I found myself in Pizza 4P’s, an ambitiously and intricately designed pizza import from Vietnam for which six literal boulders were transported into the restaurant from a stone wholesaler in New Jersey. Now three spots? There’s something going on there.

articles.title: How Mariska Hargitay Pulled Off Her Fashion-Filled 2026 Emmys Hosting Gig
articles.summary: “Let’s be honest, it’s a little terrifying,” says Harigtay of hosting. “But I’m in a season of my life where I’ve been presented with opportunities that terrified me a bit, so I thought, why not!”
body: Given the fact that Mariska Hargitay has been steering Law & Order: SVU for 27 years (!!) now, it’s safe to say she was the perfect choice to host the 2026 Emmys last night. She is, after all, a TV legend.

There was even more to celebrate: Hargitay was also the first woman to host the Emmys in 15 years. “When I first heard that, I was genuinely surprised,” Hargitay tells Vogue post-event. “Of course I understand the significance of it, and I’m incredibly proud to be that woman. But I also hope the next woman doesn’t have to wait another 15 years. There are so many brilliant, funny, fearless women who could stand on that stage.”

Her opening monologue certainly did not disappoint. “NBC is celebrating its 100th year, and I’ve been on Law & Order for all of them,” was one of many zingers. There were skits with Taylor Swift, and even a musical number with Andrew Rannells. “I love television,” Hargitay says. “I’ve spent so much of my life making it, and I very much understand how many people it takes to tell these stories and make them matter. So the idea of getting to stand in that room, and celebrate this community, felt incredibly special.”

articles.title: With ‘Book of Hours,’ Ellen O’Connell Whittet Finds a New Path to Justice
articles.summary: Ellen O’Connell Whittet speaks to Vogue about how her Catholic upbringing informed her experiences with pregnancy; fictionalizing her own story; and finding new paths to justice outside of the law.
body: At the beginning of the pandemic, author Ellen O’Connell Whittet was preparing to publish her first book and give birth to her first child. By the time her memoir, What You Become in Flight, hit shelves that April, Whittet had told her entire life story—including her challenges with an eating disorder and a ballet career cut short—with no idea what lay ahead.

When Whittet experienced an act of obstetric violence during her already arduous labor, she knew that she would one day write about it. But, she realized, the story would perhaps be better told in a work of fiction. The result is Book of Hours, out today from Dzanc Books, in which Whittet weaves together the violence that she experiences at the hands of her doctor with her protagonist’s visions of canonized saints.
“I am very clearly not the person that I’m writing about,” she says. “But [that] I could give the experience to somebody that feels like justice.”
Vogue: When did you know that you were going to write about your birth experience? When did you feel ready to write about it?
points: Ellen O’Connell Whittet speaks to Vogue about how her Catholic upbringing informed her experiences with pregnancy; fictionalizing her own story; and finding new paths to justice outside of the law.

articles.title: Family Affair: Tessa Tran Revives Chan Luu, Mixing California Ease With a Touch of Sensuality
articles.summary: Tessa Tran revives Chan Luu, mixing California ease with a touch of sensuality.
body: What goes around comes back around, and that includes the beloved 2000s jewelry brand Chan Luu. These days, the LA-born label is back under a different creative director, but not too removed from its original iteration, with Luu’s niece Tessa Tran holding the reins as the brand’s artistic director.

Tran, who started off as her aunt’s intern at the brand after graduating from FIT, has slowly risen through the ranks of the business. In 2014, after Luu sold a majority of her stake in the company to private investors, Tran stayed on, then fully bought back her family business in 2023. Since then she’s revived the once beloved boho label into a ready-to-wear brand that still has the same artisan-first mentality her aunt had 25 years ago. Everything is still made in the same factories that her aunt used in India and Vietnam. “As we’ve grown, our factories have grown with us, becoming a generational family business both for me and them,” she said.
points: Tessa Tran revives Chan Luu, mixing California ease with a touch of sensuality.

articles.title: Using This Under-Pillow Speaker Is Way More Comfortable Than Sleeping With Earbuds
articles.summary: We may earn a commission from links on this page. If you're one of those people who can't fall asleep without a " Sleep With Me " podcast droning on, or playing one of those Spotify "Sleep Music 528 Hz" playlists, this week's upgrade is for you.
body: The Jabees Peace Duo sleep speaker is one of my favorite solutions to one of my toughest problems: How do you listen to something all night, comfortably, privately, without wearing anything on or in your ears?

The Peace Duo uses my favorite audio trend, bone conduction technology (pillow conduction technology?). Typically, bone conduction devices send sound vibrations directly toward your inner ear, through the bones of your skull, instead of blasting it out through the open air or directly into your ear canals.

This speaker sits under your pillow rather than in or on your body, which is really the whole point of the "private under-pillow listening" claims. The sound stays close to your head and doesn't broadcast across the room the way a phone or bedside speaker would. Paired with a dual-speaker design, it gives you separate left and right listening units, so you get a bit of stereo positioning depending on how you're lying. Plus, it has a reliable 10-hour battery life, so you can run your sleep soundtrack all night without having to think about it.
